deep.reconstruction:
This page states and starts to prove a functorial version of what is now called Quillen's small object argument. It lives inside the 'Champs 2' notes (c. 1982), between pages that are only reused computer listings.

Setting. M is a category, possibly large. Φ is a class of arrows in M. Ψ is, as the 'Example' shows, the class of arrows with the right lifting property with respect to Φ (Ψ = Φ^⊥, presumably defined on earlier pages). Conversely Ψ* = ⊥Ψ is the class of arrows with the left lifting property with respect to Ψ. The heading appears to read 'Ex. Ulmer', most likely a pointer to Gabriel–Ulmer's theory of locally presentable categories.

Hypotheses.
(a) Φ is small (a set), and the source and target of each φ ∈ Φ are small/presentable objects. These are the objects whose Hom commutes with filtered colimits of the relevant size.
(b) M has filtered (directed) colimits.
(c) Pushouts of arrows of Φ along arbitrary maps exist and stay in Φ.
(c') Φ is closed under composition.
(d) Φ is stable under filtering direct limits. This means: if (A_i) is a directed system whose transition maps lie in Φ, then A_{i0} → colim A_i lies in Φ. A marginal note says it suffices to check this for directed posets in which any two elements have a supremum.

Conclusion. (Φ, Ψ) satisfies the factorization condition: every f : X → Y factors as X → X̃(f) → Y, with i(f) ∈ Φ and p(f) ∈ Ψ. Moreover this is functorial. There is a functor Σ : Fl(M) → Fl(M) on the arrow category, compatible with the target functor t to M, together with a natural transformation id_{Fl(M)} → Σ in [Cat]/M (possibly large categories over M). Its component at f is the square from f to p(f), whose top edge is i(f). In modern terms this is a functorial (natural) weak factorization system, produced by the small object argument.

Example. Assume M has pushouts, Φ0 is a small set of arrows, Ψ = Φ0^⊥, and Φ = Φ̄0 = Ψ* = ⊥Ψ (the saturation). Then (c) and (c') hold trivially, since left-lifting classes are closed under pushout and composition.

For (d), Grothendieck writes 'OK' and sketches a proof. Take a directed system A_{i0} → A_i → B = colim A_i with transition maps in Φ, and a lifting square: u0 : A_{i0} → X on top, v : B → Y on the bottom, f : X → Y in Ψ, with g : A_{i0} → B on the left. He wants a diagonal B → X. He applies Zorn's lemma to pairs (J ⊂ I a filtering subset, u_J : colim_J A_j → X) making the diagram A_{i0} → A_J → B over X → Y commute, ordered by extension. He then reformulates the goal: Hom(B, X) → Hom(g, f) is surjective, where Hom(g, f) = lim_i Hom(g_i, f) and g_i : A_{i0} → A_i.

The point of the whole page is to supply factorization systems (Φ, Ψ) for the stack-theoretic constructions in this manuscript. It is a pre-Pursuing-Stacks (c. 1982) encounter with the machinery of cofibrantly generated weak factorization systems.
errors: The Zorn argument for (d) is only sketched and has a genuine gap at the successor step. Given a maximal (J, u_J) with J ≠ I, one must extend to a larger filtering J' ⊃ J. This requires the comparison map colim_J A_j → colim_{J'} A_j to lie in ⊥Ψ, which is not automatic for a general directed poset. Neither left classes nor these comparison maps admit an obvious cancellation property.

For well-ordered chains the statement (closure of ⊥Ψ under transfinite composition) is standard. For arbitrary directed posets one needs an extra reduction, e.g. Iwamura's lemma (a directed poset is a union of a smooth chain of directed subsets of smaller cardinality) plus induction on cardinality. Alternatively, define (d) only for chains, which suffices for the small object argument. The marginal remark about posets with binary sups does not by itself close this gap.
Hypothesis (a) as written ('source and target accessible') is stronger than needed. Only the sources need to be small relative to the colimits used. This is harmless.

With Φ = ⊥Ψ, the factorization produced by the argument actually lands in the cell complexes on Φ0. Membership in the saturated class Φ is then automatic. Fine, but the proof that the constructed X̃(f) → Y lies in Ψ uses smallness of the sources of Φ0, not of all of Φ. The page conflates Φ0 and Φ in hypothesis (a) for the Example: Φ̄0 is not small.

ideas.what: Factorization of any arrow as (map in Φ) followed by (map with RLP w.r.t. Φ), under smallness of Φ, existence of pushouts and filtered colimits, and closure of Φ under pushout, composition and filtered colimits.
ideas.modern_name: Quillen's small object argument / cofibrantly generated weak factorization system
ideas.usually_credited_to: Quillen (Homotopical Algebra, 1967); refined by Bousfield (1977), Hovey, Hirschhorn; Gabriel–Ulmer (1971) for the accessibility framework
ideas.where_published: Possibly discussed in Pursuing Stacks (1983) in connection with Quillen model categories; not in EGA/SGA

ideas.what: Functoriality of the factorization: an endofunctor Σ of the arrow category over M (via target) with a natural transformation id → Σ in Cat/M.
ideas.modern_name: functorial (natural) weak factorization system; 'algebraic' version via Garner
ideas.usually_credited_to: Quillen / Bousfield (functorial small object argument); Grandis–Tholen (natural wfs, 2006); Garner (algebraic small object argument, 2009)

ideas.what: Saturation Φ̄0 = ⊥(Φ0^⊥) of a generating set is automatically stable under pushouts and composition; closure under directed colimits verified via a Zorn/lifting argument, rewriting Hom(B,X) → Hom(g,f) = lim Hom(g_i,f) as a surjectivity statement.
ideas.modern_name: weakly saturated class closed under transfinite composition
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard (Quillen; Hovey 'Model Categories' 1999; Lurie HTT A.1.2)

missed.claim: Historical: c. 1982, before Pursuing Stacks, Grothendieck independently formulates the functorial small object argument as a natural transformation id → Σ in Cat/M. He axiomatizes it with closure of Φ under filtering colimits rather than transfinite composition, and links it to Gabriel–Ulmer accessibility. This shows he was handling factorization-system technology in the stacks context earlier than usually documented. Mathematically it is not new.
missed.quote: Then (Φ,Ψ) satisfy the factorisation condition, and more, there exists a functor Σ : Fl(M) → Fl(M) ... and a functorial morphism id_{Fl(M)} → Σ in [Cat]/M (possibly "large" categories over M)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Of interest to historians tracing Grothendieck's engagement with Quillen-style homotopical algebra before Pursuing Stacks; no new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: A rederivation of the functorial small object argument, well known since Quillen/Bousfield and later systematized by Garner. Its interest is purely historical: it appears in pre-1983 stack notes framed in Gabriel–Ulmer terms. The closure-under-directed-colimits step is left with a gap.
transcription_corrections: Heading likely reads 'Ex. Ulmer' (reference to Gabriel–Ulmer) rather than an unknown name; uncertain.
In (a) the word read as 'accessible' may be 'small'/'accessible'; the sense is that sources/targets are small (presentable) objects.
The '{+for complete[?] limits[?]+}' insertion near 'Zorn' is probably 'for complete details' or 'for complete limits'; illegible, low confidence.
Diagram on the left: X →^{i(f)} X̃(f) →^{p(f)} Y (factorization of f), not a separate symbol φ.
The Zorn pairs are (J ⊂ I filtering subset, u_J : colim_{J} A_j → X); Hom(g,f) refers to g : A_{i0} → B and g_i : A_{i0} → A_i.
Bottom-left 'in direction[?]' is unclear; it may be a stray marginal note.
